en: I bow to you, Mother Utkala,
of lovely smile, of lovely speech,
Mother, Mother, Mother,
I bow to you, Mother Utkala.
your body washed by the holy sea,
your shores made lovely by palmyra and tamāla trees,
your breeze bearing spray from the banks of bright rivers,
Mother, Mother, Mother,
I bow to you, Mother Utkala.
your limbs made splendid by dense, dense forests,
rows of blue mountains adorning you in waves,
loud with the warbling of lovely birds,
Mother, Mother, Mother,
I bow to you, Mother Utkala.
your fields made lovely by fine rice,
your eyes showing knowledge and learning,
made holy by the huts of yogis and hosts of sages,
Mother, Mother, Mother,
I bow to you, Mother Utkala.
a land adorned with beautiful temples,
your dress made splendid by the fine arts in their rows,
your regions full of holy places of pilgrimage,
Mother, Mother, Mother,
I bow to you, Mother Utkala.
Utkala, a home made proud by the best of gods,
your body smeared with the blood of the hosts of your foes,
who have shown your noble love to the whole round of the world,
Mother, Mother, Mother,
I bow to you, Mother Utkala.
worshipped by your good sons, crowns of the race of poets [?],
your fame proclaimed through the world, beyond reproach,
O blessed one, O holy one, refuge for ever,
Mother, Mother, Mother,
I bow to you, Mother Utkala.
notes: Romanization: ISO 15919 applied to the Odia letters as written: the inherent vowel written, as Odia sounds it (jananī, śarīra); ଳ is ḷ (utkaḷa, tāḷa, nīḷa, kaḷā), distinct from ଲ l; ବ is b throughout (bande, bidhauta, biśba), as Odia writes one letter for b and v; ୟ is ẏ, ଯ y, and the subscript ya of a conjunct y (puṇya, dhanye); ଋ and its sign r̥; ଂ ṁ; doubled letters kept as written (pūrṇṇa, kīrtti, carccita). The source's hyphens are kept and the danda । is given as a full stop.

The song is in a highly Sanskritized Odia: most lines are long compounds describing the Mother, addressed as a goddess-like figure of the land (Utkala is an old name of Odisha). The compounds are unpacked in the translation in their own order where English allows.
line 1.1: bande, 'I bow to, I salute' (Sanskrit vande), as in Bankim's Vande Mataram; jananī, 'mother' (she who gives birth).
line 1.2: hāsa, 'smile, laughter'; bhāṣa, 'speech, language': 'whose smile is lovely, whose speech is lovely'.
line 2.1: paẏodhi, 'the sea' (literally 'holder of waters'); pūta, 'pure, holy'.
line 2.2: tāḷa, the palmyra palm; tamāḷa, a dark-leaved tree of Sanskrit poetry. 2.3: śīkara, fine spray; samīra, breeze; taṭinī, river.
line 3.1: rājita-aṅge, 'on limbs made splendid': the forests adorn the Mother's body. 3.2: bhūdhara, 'mountain' ('earth-holder'); 'sāje taraṅge', 'is arrayed in waves' (range behind range).
line 3.3: 'kaḷa kaḷa', the sound of many birds (or of running water); mukharita, 'made to resound'.

line 4.2: 'jñāna-bijñāna', knowledge and (practical or discerning) knowledge; 'learning' or 'science' are both possible for the second word. 'pradarśita-netra', 'whose eyes show forth' (or 'whose eyes are shown': the compound can be read either way).
line 4.3: ūṭaja, a hut of leaves, a hermitage (usually spelt uṭaja; written here with a long ū).
line 5.2: 'cāru-kaḷā-baḷi-śobhita-beśā', 'whose dress shines with rows (or the whole range) of fine arts'.
line 5.3: tīrtha, a sacred bathing-place or place of pilgrimage; caya, 'a heap, a multitude'.
line 6.1: 'sura-bara-darpita-gehā', 'whose home is proud of (or made proud by) the best of the gods'; which god is meant the line does not say.
line 6.3: 'biśba-bhūmaṇḍaḷa-kr̥ta-bara-snehā', 'by whom excellent love has been shown to the whole circle of the earth'; bara can also be read 'boon' ('who has made her love a boon to the world').

line 7.1: the sense is uncertain [?]: kabikuḷa-mauḷi, 'crown (or crest-jewel) of the race of poets', may describe the sons who honour her, a single great poet, or the Mother herself; sunandana, 'good son' (or 'one who delights'); bandyā, 'to be worshipped, worshipped'.
line 7.3: dhanye, puṇye, śaraṇye are vocatives: 'O blessed one, O holy one, O refuge'.
line 7.5: orig ends '।|', a stray bar after the danda, probably from the import; the editor may want to remove it. Romanized without it.
